newsitem.title: UK: Sleaze haunts UK Conservatives election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Sleaze haunts UK Conservatives election campaign.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major's hopes of shaking off his party's unsavoury image before a May 1 election faded on Thursday after a Conservative MP quit under pressure over allegations of influence peddling and a newspaper accused another of an affair with a teenager.
Tim Smith, a former junior Northern Ireland minister, announced he was standing down as a Conservative candidate following a row over his acceptance of cash for asking questions in parliament.

Then Sun newspaper, a long-time Tory cheerleader which last week declared its support for the opposition Labour Party, splashed its front page with reports that a Conservative member of parliament was having an affair with a 17-year-old a nightclub hostess.
The Sun published a series of colour photographs in its Thursday edition showing the married MP kissing and embracing the blonde teenager,

In 1992, the tabloid owned by media baron Rupert Murdoch, claimed it had won the election for the Conservatives. Its switch of allegiance was one of the many blows Major's party has suffered in the first week-and-a-half of its campaign to win an unprecedented fifth term of office.
The sleaze issue has repeatedly diverted attention away from Conservative efforts to pinpoint weaknesses in opposition Labour's policies.

Lagging Labour by some 25 points in opinion polls, the ruling party scored a momentary success on Wednesday, when former prime minister Margaret Thatcher accused Labour of opening the way for a resurgence of the powerful trade unions that dominated Britain in the 1970s. But its ascendance was halted by Smith's announcement.

The Conservatives also seized on Labour's announcement that it would increase spending on health by more than the rate of inflation. Wary of making high spending promises, Labour had previously declined to match the Conservatives' pledge to increase National Health Service (NHS) spending every year. "We will give the NHS more money every year, but unlike the Tories (Conservatives) we will insist that every penny of that goes not to administration but to patient care," Labour's finance spokesman said late on Wednesday.
Health minister Stephen Dorrell accused him of making a policy U-turn.
"Mr Brown and Mr (Labour leader Tony) Blair have always refused to match this pledge, now they recognise they have lost the argument," Dorrell said.
But Labour is sure to turn the argument back to sleaze. It has accused Major of dismissing parliament early to avoid publication of a report into the cash for questions row.

A partial report presented to parliament last week found several members of parliament implicated in the cash for questions row innocent of any wrongdoing, but ten Conservatives, including Smith, have yet to be cleared.
Smith blamed an unjust media campaign for driving him out of the election race, although he has admitted he failed to declare in the register of MPs outside earnings cash payments he received from

"I very much regret that the action of the Guardian newspaper in support of the Labour party has made my course of action inevitable with its complete disregard of both parliamentary privilege and natural justice," Smith said.
